name: Algorithm Distillation (AD) - In-context Reinforcement Learning with Algorithm Distillation
venue: ICLR 2023 (notable-top-5% / Oral). Published on OpenReview 01 Feb 2023 (id=hy0a5MMPUv). Preprint arXiv:2210.14215 (cs.LG; cs.AI), submitted 25 Oct 2022 (v1). Also presented at the NeurIPS 2022 'Foundation Models for Decision Making' workshop.
authors_affiliation: Michael Laskin, Luyu Wang, Junhyuk Oh, Emilio Parisotto, Stephen Spencer, Richie Steigerwald, DJ Strouse, Steven Hansen, Angelos Filos, Ethan Brooks, Maxime Gazeau, Himanshu Sahni, Satinder Singh, Volodymyr Mnih. All at DeepMind (now Google DeepMind). Michael Laskin is the corresponding author; equal-contribution markers are noted in the paper.
code_url: N/A (no official open-source code or models released by the authors at publication; the paper provides a project page/figures but not a public repository). Multiple unofficial reimplementations exist, e.g. https://github.com/cinemere/ad-icrl and the related corl-team/ad-eps (the latter is the official repo for the follow-up 'In-Context RL from Noise Distillation', not for AD itself). [uncertain]
task_domain: Decision-making / reinforcement learning (sequential decision-making in partially observed environments requiring exploration, temporal credit assignment, and generalization). It is an in-context / meta-RL method realized with a causal transformer; spans bandits, 2D grid POMDPs, and pixel-based 3D navigation.
problem_setting: Offline, in-context (gradient-free) meta-reinforcement learning. Two-phase setup: (Phase 1, OFFLINE data generation) for each of N tasks sampled from a task distribution, an independent single-task source RL algorithm (UCB / A3C / DQN) is trained from scratch until convergence and its FULL across-episode learning history (sequences of observation-action-reward tokens spanning policy improvement) is saved to a dataset D. (Phase 2, distillation) a causal transformer is trained by autoregressively predicting actions from multi-episodic subsequences of these histories with a negative-log-likelihood (behaviour-cloning) loss; crucially the context must be large enough (across-episodic) to capture learning progress, forcing the model to amortise the policy-improvement operator. (Phase 3, EVALUATION) on held-out test tasks the frozen transformer is unrolled in the environment, maintaining a running context queue of its own state-action-reward transitions, and improves its policy entirely IN-CONTEXT across successive episodes with NO weight updates, no demonstrations, and no return conditioning (it conditions on rewards, not desired returns). Single-agent; supervision is the source RL agent's own trajectories (no human labels); environments are partially observed, sparse/semi-sparse reward, with tasks that cannot be inferred zero-shot from observations.
what_is_retrieved: Across-episode learning histories / trajectories: the transformer's context is filled with the agent's own preceding (observation, action, reward) transitions across multiple recent episodes. The 'retrieved' / conditioned-on memory is the in-context running history of the current evaluation episode(s), and at training time multi-episodic subsequences of source-RL learning histories. There is no external document/case retriever; conditioning is via the transformer's attention over its context window.
retrieval_grounding: GROWING / episodic in-context memory (the transformer's own context window) rather than a static external corpus. At test time the model writes its own (o,a,r) transitions into a rolling context queue and attends back over them; this self-generated within-deployment history is what drives in-context improvement. The training data D (offline learning histories from source RL) is a fixed, offline-induced store used only to train the transformer's weights, not queried at inference. So the operative 'memory' is a context-window episodic buffer, not a retrieval-from-corpus mechanism. [uncertain] (Borderline: AD is an in-context-RL precursor whose 'retrieval' is attention over its own context rather than an explicit retriever over a store.)
completeness_vs_topk_objective: N/A / not a ranking objective. AD does not rank or select top-k items; instead it conditions on the entire (sliding-window) across-episode context. The relevant design choice is context LENGTH (must be multi-episodic, ~2-4 episodes) rather than a top-k selection or completeness criterion.
retrieval_unit: (state, action, reward) tuple stream, i.e. (o_t, a_t, r_t) transition tokens, organized as across-episode sub-trajectories. The conditioning unit is a multi-episodic subsequence of length c (spanning >= 1, ideally 2-4 episodes) of these transition tuples; it is reward-conditioned (not return-conditioned).
index_source: Offline-induced fixed dataset for training (the buffer D of source-RL learning histories), plus an online/test-time-induced episodic context at inference (the transformer's own rolling context of (o,a,r) tuples). No retrievable external store; the 'index' is effectively the transformer's context window populated online during evaluation.
index_structure_topology: N/A in the classic sense: there is no vector index or graph. The store is a flat sequential buffer/context of (o,a,r) tokens consumed by a causal transformer via positional/causal attention. Training subsequences are sampled uniformly from histories; evaluation maintains a FIFO context queue.
retriever_type: N/A (no explicit retriever). Conditioning is performed implicitly by the causal transformer's self-attention over the in-context history (GPT-like decoder-only sequence model). No BM25/dense/learned retriever.
retriever_learning_signal: N/A for an external retriever. The sequence model itself (which functionally subsumes the role of selecting/attending to relevant context) is trained end-to-end by a negative-log-likelihood / behaviour-cloning loss on next-action prediction over the source-RL learning histories. So the 'attention-as-retrieval' is learned by imitation (NLL on actions), not by similarity contrastive labels, RL reward, or downstream-task preference.
query_construction: The 'query' is the current across-episode context: the most recent (o,a,r) transitions in the rolling context queue, with the current observation as the immediate conditioning input. No decomposition, intent extraction, or synthetic expansion; the raw running history is the conditioning signal.
query_granularity: step/state-level (autoregressive): at every timestep the model conditions on the full current across-episode context to predict the next action; effectively continuous per-step conditioning that also spans trajectory/multi-episode level via the long context window.
when_to_retrieve: iterative / continuous: conditioning happens at every action step throughout the rollout, with the context continuously updated by the agent's own newest transitions. It is not a one-shot retrieve-then-act; in-context improvement accrues across many episodes.
retrieval_trigger_signal: fixed schedule (every step): the model attends to its context window at each decision step automatically. There is no confidence/uncertainty/learned-classifier/reflection-token trigger and no agent-initiated retrieval request; conditioning is unconditional and continuous, governed only by the sliding context window.
reranking: None. No reranking stage; the causal transformer attends over the whole context window without an explicit candidate re-scoring step.
retrieved_context_refinement: None / minimal: context is the raw (o,a,r) token stream truncated to the across-episodic window length c (a sliding/FIFO window because attention is quadratic in sequence length). No compression, distillation, decomposition, or distractor filtering of the context beyond windowing.
how_retrieved_used: Latent / in-context conditioning for action generation: the across-episode history is fed as the transformer's context and the model autoregressively predicts the next action, implicitly inferring the (improved) policy from the conditioning history. Used as input context (in-context learning), NOT as a training signal at inference, NOT as prompt-engineered text, and NOT via fine-tuning (weights are frozen at test time).
planning_integration: Inside an autoregressive control loop (per-step interleaved): there is no explicit planner/tree-search; the transformer directly maps the across-episode context to the next action at every step, and 'planning'/exploration/credit-assignment behaviours emerge implicitly from having distilled an RL algorithm's improvement operator. Conditioning and acting are tightly interleaved per timestep across a multi-episode horizon (retrieve/condition then act, continuously).
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: per-step (per-action / per-timestep): the context is consulted and an action emitted at every environment step, with the context growing as the agent acts; improvement is realized across episodes. Not per-CoT-step (no explicit chain-of-thought) and not per-tool-call.
retrieved_item_representation: Raw trajectory tokens: the injected/conditioned representation is the raw sequence of (observation, action, reward) tokens of the agent's recent across-episode history (pixels/coordinates as observations, discrete actions, scalar rewards). No distilled strategy text, no executable program, no structured note; it is the raw experience stream consumed by the transformer.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Raw trajectory / raw experience tuples (the lowest abstraction level): the unit conditioned on is the concrete (o,a,r) transition history. Abstraction (the policy-improvement operator) lives in the LEARNED WEIGHTS of the transformer, not in the conditioned-on units, which remain raw.
noise_robustness_mechanism: Trained-in robustness via imitating an RL algorithm's improvement operator (the model learns to explore/exploit and ignore uninformative reward-0 transitions, e.g. in Dark Room Hard where reward is r=1 exactly once). The paper adds label-smoothing regularization for the hard-exploration variant (Dark Room Hard) to improve in-context learning. No explicit relevance evaluator, self-reflection, or distractor filter; robustness is emergent from distillation plus the across-episodic context that lets it infer goals from sparse signals.
memory_type: latent + episodic: the policy-improvement algorithm is stored latently in the transformer weights (in-weights RL algorithm amortised into an in-context one), while the operative test-time memory is an episodic across-episode context buffer of the agent's own (o,a,r) transitions. No external skill-library, workflow store, or graph.
write_back: Yes, but only into the transient in-context buffer, not a persistent external store. During evaluation the agent appends its own (o,a,r) transitions to the rolling context queue (which drives in-context improvement); these are discarded at episode/window boundaries. There is NO write-back of new cases/skills to a persistent memory and NO weight update at test time.
online_growth: Partial / context-only: the in-context history grows online during a deployment rollout (across episodes within the context window) and is what enables test-time improvement, but it is a bounded sliding window and is reset per evaluation; there is no persistent growing store and no parameter growth. The training dataset D is frozen after offline collection.
write_back_trigger: per-step (into the rolling context only): each new (o,a,r) transition is automatically appended to the context queue at every timestep during a rollout (then truncated by the window). There is no success/failure-gated, reflective, or human-validated write into any persistent memory; nothing is permanently retained.
failure_experience_usage: Both successes and failures are used implicitly and uniformly: training histories include the entire learning curve of the source RL algorithm (early failed/low-reward episodes through to converged success), and at test time the model conditions on its own successful AND unsuccessful (reward-0) episodes within the context, which is precisely how it explores and infers sparse goals. There is no explicit contrastive success-vs-failure mechanism or failure-only corrective rule store; failures are valuable as part of the learning-progress signal that teaches the improvement operator.
memory_evolution_update: Append-and-forget (sliding window): the in-context buffer is append-only within a window and forgotten (FIFO truncation) once the across-episodic context length c is exceeded; no dedup-merge, delta-update, or refine-overwrite of stored entries. The latent algorithm (weights) is fixed after distillation.
retrieval_as_learned_policy: No external learned retrieval policy. However, the in-context behaviour IS a learned (distilled) policy-improvement operator: the transformer is trained by imitation (NLL) to reproduce an RL algorithm's improvement dynamics, so 'how to use context' is learned, but it is not an RL/value-optimized retrieval/selection policy over an external store. Selection over context is implicit attention, not an explicit top-k or learned retriever.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: No. Single-agent, single-model in-context memory. (The offline training dataset is aggregated from many independent single-task source-RL runs/actors, and AD distills a multi-stream distributed algorithm into a single-stream one, but the deployed AD agent uses its own private context; there is no cross-agent memory sharing at inference.)
benchmarks: Adversarial Bandit (10-armed bandit, 100 trials, reward under odd arms 95% of the time in training vs even arms 95% at evaluation; out-of-distribution test), Dark Room (2D discrete POMDP, 9x9 room, episode length 20, dense reward r=1 each time goal reached), Dark Room (Hard) (17x17 room, sparse reward r=1 exactly once), Dark Key-to-Door (9x9, must reach an invisible key then door, semi-sparse reward, episode length 50, combinatorial task space of 81^2 = 6561 tasks), and DMLab Watermaze (partially observable 3D pixel-based navigation, observations 72x96x3, 8 actions, episode length 50, continuous/infinite goal space).
benchmark_family: decision-RL / meta-RL control environments (bandits + grid-world POMDPs + DMLab pixel navigation). Not in the survey's QA/web/embodied-benchmark/tool families; closest tag is decision-RL (custom RL environments, not D4RL).
baselines: Expert Distillation (ED) - identical architecture/across-episode context to AD but trained on EXPERT (converged-policy) trajectories instead of full learning histories (closest analog to Gato but reward-conditioned); RL^2 (Duan et al. 2016) - an online meta-RL algorithm trained for 1B environment steps, used as an approximate upper bound (also compared with transformer vs LSTM backbones); the SOURCE RL algorithm run from scratch (UCB / A3C / DQN) - to compare data-efficiency of in-context RL vs the in-weights source. Decision-Transformer-style return-conditioned PD (MGDT, Gato) discussed as related work / context, with ED serving as the implemented PD-style baseline.
key_metrics: Episodic return / accumulated reward as a function of evaluation episode number (in-context learning curves), reported as mean return +/- 1 standard deviation over 5 training seeds; scores often normalized relative to UCB (bandit) and random/source. Data-efficiency is measured as episodes/environment-steps needed to reach a performance level vs the source algorithm. No retrieval-IR metrics (Recall@k / nDCG) since there is no retrieval benchmark.
headline_result: Algorithm Distillation reinforcement-learns entirely in-context (no weight updates) across all environments and is more data-efficient than the source RL algorithm it distilled. AD matches asymptotic RL^2 (an online meta-RL upper-bound trained for 1B steps) on the Dark environments and approaches it to within 13% on DMLab Watermaze, whereas Expert Distillation (ED) fails to explore/improve in-context in most settings. AD also generalizes out-of-distribution on the Adversarial Bandit better than RL^2 and ED. By distilling a multi-stream distributed source algorithm into a single-stream in-context one (and in a single-stream subsample-every-k=10 setting), AD produces a faster/more data-efficient RL algorithm than the source that generated its training data.
ablations: (1) Context size (Fig.7, Dark Key-to-Door / Dark Room): in-context RL only emerges with multi-episodic context; ~2-4 episodes of context are needed for near-optimal in-context RL, with initial signs appearing once context >= ~1 episode length - the central ablation establishing that across-episodic context, not just learning-history data, is required. (2) AD vs ED (same architecture/context, different data): isolates that benefits come from training on LEARNING HISTORIES (showing learning progress) rather than from long context alone; ED collapses to near-random/expert-imitation without in-context improvement. (3) Single-stream Algorithm Distillation (Fig.6, App.I): subsampling every k-th (k=10) episode from a single A3C actor's history still yields a more data-efficient in-context algorithm than both the multi-stream and single-stream source. (4) Source-algorithm-agnosticism: AD distills UCB (bandit), on-policy A3C (Dark envs), and off-policy DQN (Watermaze). (5) Architecture: AD can also be realized with an LSTM (App.K) but less effectively than a causal transformer; RL^2 with transformer vs LSTM compared (App.G). (6) Label smoothing improves AD on the hard-exploration Dark Room (Hard) (App. with Fig.10).
evaluation_decoupling: N/A. No intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k/nDCG/completeness) are reported because there is no explicit retriever; evaluation is end-to-end in-context-RL learning curves (return vs episode).
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Both outcome and process: primary metric is episodic return (outcome), but the paper also analyses the in-context LEARNING PROCESS via per-episode learning curves (how return improves across successive evaluation episodes), and probes specific capabilities - in-context exploration (Dark Room Hard), temporal credit assignment, and in-distribution / out-of-distribution generalization (Dark Key-to-Door combinatorial tasks; Adversarial Bandit OOD).
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Data-efficiency is the headline efficiency claim: AD is significantly more data-efficient (fewer episodes to reach performance) than the source RL algorithm, turning a slow gradient-based learner into a faster in-context learner. Cost caveat: transformer training and inference are quadratic in sequence length, and because environments of interest have long episodes, AD requires fitting multiple episodes into the context window, which is the main stated limitation/cost; this restricts AD to short-episode environments and motivates long-horizon sequence models as future work. No explicit dollar/latency numbers reported.
context_budget_and_selection_count: Budget set by the across-episodic context length c (sampled subsequences of length c < full history T at training; a FIFO context queue at evaluation). The key budget rule is that the context must span multiple episodes (empirically ~2-4 episodes) for in-context RL to emerge; specific token/c values vary per environment (episode lengths 20-50 steps; e.g. Dark Room episode length 20, Key-to-Door/Watermaze 50). Not a fixed-k item selection - it is a window-length (multi-episode) budget. [uncertain] (exact c per environment in tokens is in the appendix hyperparameter tables).
benchmark_construction_and_size: N/A (introduces/uses custom RL environments rather than a curated benchmark dataset: Adversarial Bandit 10 arms/100 trials; Dark Room 9x9 ep20; Dark Room Hard 17x17 sparse; Dark Key-to-Door 9x9 ep50 with 6561 tasks; DMLab Watermaze pixel 72x96x3 ep50. Training data: 2000 A3C learning histories (100 actors) for Dark envs, 4000 distributed-DQN histories (16 actors) for Watermaze.)
cbr_cycle_coverage: [Retrieve: partial (attention over the in-context history substitutes for explicit case retrieval), Reuse: yes (conditions on past experience to choose actions / amortises the improvement operator), Revise: no (no explicit case adaptation/critique step), Retain: partial (transient append to the rolling context only; no persistent case retention)]. AD is not a CBR system; mapping is loose.
explicit_cbr_grounding: False. The paper frames itself as in-context reinforcement learning / offline in-context meta-RL / algorithm distillation via sequence modeling (citing RL^2, MAML, Decision Transformer, Gato, policy distillation). It does NOT cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner and does not invoke case-based reasoning.
index_content_separation: N/A (no separated lightweight index vs heavy content; the context is the raw token stream).
dynamic_index_and_protocol: N/A (not a tool-retrieval system; agent interacts with RL environments / DMLab, not tool APIs/MCP).
adaptation_mechanism: N/A in the CBR sense; the closest analog is that the LEARNED in-context policy-improvement operator adapts behaviour across episodes by conditioning on accumulated experience (verbatim raw-history conditioning, not LLM-prompted case adaptation or execution-feedback revision). No explicit per-case adaptation/critique.
builds_on: RL^2 / fast-RL-via-slow-RL in-context meta-RL (Duan et al. 2016; Wang et al. 2016); Decision Transformer (Chen et al. 2021) and Trajectory Transformer (Janner et al. 2021) sequence-modeling-for-RL; Multi-Game Decision Transformer (Lee et al. 2022) and Gato (Reed et al. 2022) as policy-distillation predecessors; Policy Distillation (Rusu et al. 2016, here from offline data); source RL algorithms UCB (Lai & Robbins 1985), A3C (Mnih et al. 2016), DQN (Mnih et al. 2013); causal transformer / GPT-style sequence models; DMLab (Beattie et al. 2016) and Morris Watermaze (Morris 1981).
contrasts_with: Offline Policy Distillation (PD) methods - MGDT (return-conditioned, adapts by finetuning) and Gato (adapts via expert-demonstration prompting), and its own Expert Distillation (ED) baseline - all of which learn policies but NOT an RL algorithm and cannot improve in-context through trial-and-error because their contexts are within-episode (too short to capture learning progress); Decision Transformer (return-conditioned, small within-episode context); online meta-RL such as RL^2 (interacts with the env during training; used as an upper-bound proxy rather than a directly comparable method); gradient-based / optimization-based meta-RL (MAML-style) that adapts by taking gradient steps (AD is gradient-free at test time).
lineage: Group F (decision / memory / RL). Foundational in-context-RL precursor: AD is the first method to demonstrate in-context reinforcement learning via sequence modeling of offline RL learning histories with an imitation loss, sitting in the lineage RL^2 / Decision Transformer / Gato -> Algorithm Distillation -> later in-context-RL works (e.g. Decision-Pretrained Transformer, In-Context RL from Noise Distillation, DICP). It established that conditioning a causal transformer on across-episode experience (a precursor to retrieval/experience-conditioned agents) yields gradient-free policy improvement, motivating later experience/episodic-memory-augmented decision agents.
